Outcome: Depression cases (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: Service members diagnosed with vitamin D deficiency were more likely to have a depression diagnosis, including after adjustment.
Sentence: "After adjustment, vitamin D deficient diagnoses remained significantly associated with depression diagnoses (OR = 1.22; 95% CI, 1.11-1.33, p < 0.001)."
Measured as: depression diagnosis (diagnostic codes)
Population: Military service members (tactical athletes) in a retrospective records review
Intervention: Vitamin D deficiency diagnosis (observed exposure, not administered)
Comparator: Service members without a vitamin D deficiency diagnosis
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: not reported
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: harm
Claim: Vitamin D level was significantly related to risk of depression (PHQ-9 above 5) six months after COVID-19 hospital admission; the direction is not stated in the abstract.
Sentence: "The variables that were significantly related to the risk of depression 6 months after admission for COVID-19 were frailty (p = 0.006 for pre-frail and p = 0.001 for frail), small-vessel vascular disease in imaging tests (p = 0.033), vitamin D level (p = 0.006), and taking antidepressants (p = 0.011)."
Measured as: risk of depression (PHQ-9 above 5)
Population: 72 patients admitted to a hospital in Spain for COVID-19, assessed at discharge and six months later
Intervention: Serum vitamin D level (measured, not administered)
Comparator: Lower versus higher vitamin D levels across participants
Design: cohort study
Sample size: 72
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

{
  "rationale": "The two observational studies differ across multiple domains, most notably in their populations (military service members versus hospitalized COVID-19 patients), outcome measures (diagnostic codes versus PHQ-9 > 5), and designs (cross-sectional versus 6-month cohort).",
